text: Sold as a girl into a house she did not choose, she becomes the one who decides who works in it and on what terms. The rise-through-the-ranks shape comes from crime pictures, but the territory is a few streets of brothels, and the authority she assembles rests on nothing a court would honor: no deed, no office, only favors owed by men with their own reasons to keep paying. Nobody hands her any of it. Every increment of standing is negotiated with someone who could take it back. Sanjay Leela Bhansali takes 157 minutes over the slow business of becoming a person whose calls get returned, and the film is clearest about the cost when the money is welcome and the company is not. Respectability is the single commodity here that cannot be purchased, so the scenes that hold are the ones where cash changes hands and nothing else does.

Rank matters in this romance the way it seldom does elsewhere: he is an officer in one country's air force, she is a citizen of the other. The meeting itself is almost ordinary — a bus goes off the road, a stranded traveler needs help, a pilot gives it — and everything after has to contend with a line on a map that neither of them drew. Yash Chopra takes 192 minutes, which in Hindi popular cinema is not indulgence but architecture: the songs carry weight the dialogue is never asked to, and the music direction was honored on its own account. The question underneath is whether an attachment made in a few days can outlast borders and paperwork drawn up with no interest in it. Chopra makes the waiting long, and the waiting is the material.

The minor leagues run on the difference between a player with a future and a player with a job. Crash Davis is the second kind, a veteran catcher sent to Durham to finish raising a pitching prospect, which means handing a younger man the craft he himself was never quite good enough at. Annie Savoy complicates it by setting her sights on both of them, and the triangle is conducted mostly in argument. Ron Shelton fills the film with talk — about pitching, about superstition, about what a body is for once the sport has finished with it — and took the Writers Guild's original screenplay award for it. Comedy, mostly, and generous to everyone in it. Under the jokes sits the gap between being good at something and being young enough for that to be worth anything to anyone.

An eight-year-old's inheritance from her mother is an instruction: find the woman who loved her father back in college, and bring her home. The machinery is unhidden, and Karan Johar's bet is that an audience will forgive any contrivance if what arrives on the other side of it is real feeling. 185 minutes across two periods, a campus and a household, and the earlier half does the heavier work: affection filed under friendship because nobody wants to risk the other word for it, a joke that lands wrong, years going by while the thing stays unsaid. The later half is a child's project, pursued with the seriousness children bring to adult business. For a film that starts in bereavement, it spends most of its length being funny, and the comedy is not a way around the grief.

In 2001, on a train somewhere in rural India, two brides are swapped and go home with the wrong men. The mix-up needs a world in which a woman can be delivered to a household without anyone looking hard at her face, and Kiran Rao lets that single fact do double duty as the engine of the farce and the reason it stings. What follows runs on two tracks, each woman among strangers who owe her nothing and are free to be kind or not. The comedy is generous and the arrangement it describes is not. It took Filmfare's best film with a story whose largest crisis is a missed stop and a wrong address. 123 minutes, broad where it wants to be and quiet where that serves better, and the running joke is how fast everyone else decides whose problem two misplaced women are.

A film about the man who conquered half the world spends its length on the years when he was owned by other people. Sergei Bodrov keeps the slave, not the khan, as the working subject: captivity, obligation, the long apprenticeship in reading whose loyalty can be bought and whose cannot. The production is itself a border case — German money, Russian dialogue, the steppe as the only landscape that counts — and the budget goes into weather and distance rather than speeches. The genre labels say war and action; it plays more like a ledger of debts, where a favor and a life are the same instrument and both come due. 125 minutes, and the distances are allowed to be distances. What it finally watches is a man calculating, over and over, what he owes and to whom.

The fire chief of a small town has decided in advance that he will not ask, and the decision is older than the woman it concerns. Rostand's play gets relocated to the Pacific Northwest and a fire station, which turns out to be the right size for it: where everyone already knows everyone's face, a face is a fact that cannot be argued with. What C. D. Bales has instead is language, and Fred Schepisi treats the fluency as defense and trap at once — the man is never more himself than when he is supplying another man's lines to a woman who believes she is hearing someone else. The Writers Guild gave its adapted screenplay award to a comedy assembled out of borrowed words, which has a certain symmetry. 107 minutes, light on the surface, and it never mistakes charm for a solution.

The obstacle here is not an army but a household that declines to receive her. Bajirao is married when he meets Mastani, and Kashibai, who has done nothing, is the one whose position erodes: a second woman's arrival costs the first her standing in rooms she has always occupied. Sanjay Leela Bhansali stages most of the conflict indoors, where the weapons are seating order, forms of address, and permission to attend. A court can refuse a person without ever speaking to her. Whatever fighting the story contains is simpler than a family meal. 158 minutes of a romance whose actual subject is protocol, and the film is most exact when no voice is raised and a woman is informed, politely and completely, of her new place.

A severed hand wakes in a dissection lab, works its way loose, and sets out across town to find the body it came from. The animation refuses to let that become a gag: the hand moves the way a small animal moves, by touch and by risk, and the suspense is a plain matter of grip. Elsewhere in the city there is Naoufel, in love with Gabrielle, and that half is told so plainly that at first the two seem to belong to different films. Jérémy Clapin needs 81 minutes for both. The Cristal at Annecy went to it, and the reason is legible in any half-minute: memory is not narrated here, it is handled — sound, texture, the weight of objects picked up and put down. The premise sounds like a stunt. It is closer to a study of touch.

The hero takes bribes, and the film asks the audience to like him for it. Chulbul Pandey's corruption arrives as a symptom rather than a flaw — a younger half-brother he is at odds with, a stepfather he could never square with, and then a uniform that makes a man untouchable. The crooked politician the plot supplies is less an antagonist than an occasion. What Abhinav Kashyap is really staging is posture: the walk, the timing of a line, a flat refusal to be embarrassed by anything, for 130 minutes at a pitch of total self-belief. The family material underneath is played straight, and it keeps the swagger from floating free of the ground. Comedy, action, and a grudge older than either. Beyond how much it enjoys its own company, the film argues nothing.

The title belongs to the patient; the point of view belongs to the doctor who has to watch. Bhaskar Bannerjee treats the poor of a city that keeps producing more of them, and the trouble with him is not that he has hardened but that he has not: the suffering still reaches him, which is a poor qualification for the work. Then a man with a terminal diagnosis is put in his care and behaves as though the arrangement ran the other way, consoling, talking, filling every room he enters. 1971, 122 minutes, essentially two men and a distance neither can close. Hrishikesh Mukherjee lets the cheerfulness stay visibly a performance, which is why the sentiment the premise invites never quite seals over. What stays is the position the doctor is put in: asked to be professional about the one thing he cannot be professional about.

213 minutes for a marriage that begins as a treaty and has to turn into something else. The order of operations is the whole interest: the wedding is a clause in an agreement between two courts, and the courtship other films spend a first act on has to be conducted afterward, by two people already bound and each answerable to relatives who would not mind seeing the other fail. Ashutosh Gowariker takes the scale seriously, which here means ceremony, delay, and long stretches in which nothing can be said directly because everything said is reported to somebody. Each private gesture also has a public reading. He cannot order what he wants. She cannot refuse without a bill arriving for someone else. Slow by design, and the negotiation is where the film lives.
